docs.title: panAtlas
docs.text:
panAtlas is a reference atlas for multi-modal evaluation across every domain of knowledge. Medicine is where its holdings run deepest today, but the atlas is not a medical atlas: each domain is mapped the same way, as a provenance-first knowledge graph that links concepts, datasets, models, their training curricula and the benchmarks that measure them. With that map, an evaluation can say where in the domain it was measured, on what and for whom, instead of reporting one context-blind number.

It is a distributed system that runs on Cresco. Every registered dataset is managed by its own Cresco plugin running beside the data, at the site that holds it. The managers report structure, never content, up the mesh to one atlas. Shared infrastructure therefore also means shared datasets and one global understanding of them, while every dataset stays where it is, under its owner's control.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Provenance first. Every fact says where it came from, and every number says when it was measured.
  • Describe once, evaluate many times. A dataset, model or benchmark is described once, as metadata, and every evaluation refers to that description.
  • Blanks are tracked as rigorously as facts. "We do not know what this model was trained on" is a recorded, comparable property, not a gap in a table.
  • Structure crosses the wire, content does not. Federation carries identifiers, counts, edges and hashes. Documents, images and protected data never leave their site.
  • Comparable only within one space. Embeddings are compared only within one registered (modality, model, version) space. Everything else joins through shared identifiers.

Purpose and principles has the full statement.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Understand the system: Architecture, then Distributed system.
  • Connect a site or a dataset: Participating agents and Wire contract.
  • Use or extend the metadata: Metadata overview.
  • Run it: Build pipeline and Operations.

How this documentation is kept honest

Each page says whether something is built, measured or only designed, and dates its numbers. Where a design document and the code disagree, the page describes what the code does and marks the difference with a warning. The sources are the panAtlas repositories (ThePanAtlas/panatlas, cresco-panatlas, agent-deployment) at the commit named in the page, plus the dated project record.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: panAtlas has two architectures that need to be kept apart: the target design (a git-backed, federated markdown fact-graph rendered to a static site) and what runs today (a build pipeline that compiles JSON registries and a property graph, served by a WordPress plugin). This page describes both, how data moves from acquisition to the site, and where each part runs.

docs.title: Data flow: from acquisition to the site
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph SRC["Upstream sources"]
    HF[(Hugging Face,<br/>TCIA, GDC, GEO, …)]
    OKN[(NSF OKN<br/>SPARQL endpoints)]
    WM[(Wikimedia dumps)]
    PM[(PubMed)]
  end
  subgraph HPC["HPC cluster (Slurm)"]
    ACQ["acquisition/*<br/>fetch · verify · DONE"]
    MAN["dataset_manifest.py<br/>manifest_hash"]
    DOC["document index,<br/>concept mapping,<br/>embeddings, evals"]
    RDF["build_rdf.py →<br/>qlever_build.py"]
    QL[("QLever store<br/>panatlas-okn")]
  end
  subgraph WS["Repository + workstation (web/)"]
    REG["registries<br/>datasets.json · models.json"]
    ATL["atlas/ markdown<br/>concept spine"]
    BLD["graph builders +<br/>build_all.sh"]
    OUT["plugin data/*.json"]
  end
  subgraph WEB["Web host"]
    WP["panatlas.net<br/>(WordPress plugin)"]
    AS["Astral agent"]
    LIT["literature cron"]
  end
  HF --> ACQ --> MAN --> REG
  OKN --> ACQ
  WM --> DOC
  ACQ --> DOC --> BLD
  REG --> BLD
  ATL --> BLD
  BLD --> OUT -- "deploy.sh" --> WP
  OUT --> AS
  OUT --> RDF --> QL
  ACQ -- "proven mirrors" --> QL
  AS -- "forced-command SSH" --> QL
  PM --> LIT --> WP

Read the flow left to right:

  1. Acquire. Each source has its own fetcher on the cluster that resumes, verifies every file, and writes a completion record only when the copy is complete (Acquisition).
  2. Register. A dataset gets a registry entry with a URN, licence and access class, and an audit manifest whose hash pins the exact version on disk (Dataset registry, Manifests). Fold and register scripts write it into web/datasets.json.
  3. Build. Heavy analysis runs on the cluster (document-to-concept mapping, embeddings, evaluation ingest). Its JSON outputs come to the repository, where the graph builders compile the served property graph and catalogs, and build_all.sh layers the curation passes on top and verifies the result (Build pipeline).
  4. Serve. deploy.sh copies the served JSON and the front-end assets to the plugin on the web host. The site reads static files at request time; nothing on the cluster is called by a page view.
  5. Query. The same graph is exported to RDF and loaded, with the OKN mirrors, into a SPARQL store on the cluster. Astral reaches the store; the public site exposes only the store's manifest (Knowledge store).

docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant WP as WordPress plugin
  participant F as data/*.json (static)
  participant P as Private assets<br/>(outside docroot)
  participant L as Hosted LLM endpoint
  participant A as Astral agent
  participant Q as SPARQL client on cluster
  B->>WP: GET /wp-json/panatlas/v1/graph (nonce, signed in)
  WP->>F: read graph.json
  WP-->>B: JSON
  B->>WP: GET universe-asset / wikimap-asset / literature
  WP->>P: stream file
  B->>WP: POST navigate {query}
  WP->>F: retrieve subgraph
  WP->>L: subgraph + query (JSON-schema constrained)

  A->>F: read the same JSON files directly
  A->>Q: base64 JSON over forced-command SSH
  Q-->>A: rows (≤ 1,000)

Three properties follow from this shape:

  • The site is a reader of files. The WordPress database holds users, options and the audit log, not the atlas. The atlas is the JSON in the plugin's data/ directory plus large assets outside the web root.
  • The cluster is never on a page view's critical path. The only runtime call outside the web host is the Navigator and model lens to the hosted LLM endpoint. Astral's SPARQL and coverage tools are the exceptions on the agent side, and they go over a restricted SSH key, not an inbound port.
  • Two front doors with one data source. The plugin's REST routes and the Astral agent read the same files; the agent does not call WordPress (web/astral/atlas_store.py).

docs.title: The architecture pivot
docs.text:
The first plan (PLAN_v1_wordpress.md, now history) built panAtlas as a WordPress application: custom post types for nodes and datasets, custom MySQL tables for edges and runs, WordPress roles, and a pre-write veto filter. On 2026-07-26 the owner replaced the substrate with a federated markdown graph on the Atlas model (ARCHITECTURE.md). The reason given is that a relational database behind an application server is single-tenant: it cannot be forked, diffed, merged, or split by community, so community-scoped facts cannot federate.

WordPress plan Federated markdown design Custom post types (pa_node, pa_dataset, …) Typed markdown pages, one file per node Edge table Typed wikilink lists in frontmatter Runs table Out-of-graph append-only run store, plus verified result- summary pages WordPress roles and capabilities Git organisation and team membership, branch protection, CODEOWNERS Pre-write veto filter Linter in an editor hook and a required CI check on every pull request REST API on WordPress Static site (read), git pull requests (write), generated JSON (agents) ORCID via a WordPress plugin ORCID via OIDC on the git host

The conceptual model survives unchanged: the curriculum graph, the jurisdiction-parameterised education ladder, the six stratification axes, the assessment framework, the provenance ethos, ORCID identity and Wikipedia seeding. PLAN.md (the current plan) builds on this decision and adds the two-layer design: a human-readable layer of concept and document pages and a machine-readable layer of atomic fact- and entity- pages (Graph schema).

docs.title: What actually runs today
docs.text:
The pivot is a design decision, not a migration that has happened

As of the repository at 57505c6 the live system is still a WordPress plugin serving JSON. Specifically:

  • WordPress serves the site. The panatlas-explorer plugin (version 0.2.2) registers the REST routes, shortcodes, roles and audit table; MySQL holds users and the panatlas_audit table.
  • The property graph is compiled from JSON registries and cluster outputs, not rendered from the markdown vault. web/build_layered.py reads the atlas/20-concepts/ pages for the concept spine; the remaining atlas/ page types (facts, entities, items) are not yet in the served graph.
  • No CI, git-host ORCID login, pull-request verification or static renderer exists in the repository. atlas/tools/lint_panatlas.py and atlas/tools/seed_wikipedia.py are the two built tools.
  • No page in atlas/ is verified.
  • Writes are proposals. POST /panatlas/v1/propose records a proposal in the audit log for a curator; it edits nothing.

The graph standards adopted the same day (GRAPH_STANDARDS.md) describe the served graph.json as a projection of an RDF graph, not a separate source of truth. That RDF form now exists: web/rdf/build_rdf.py exports the served graph as N-Quads, and the SPARQL store holds it.

docs.title: Layers of the graph
docs.text: GRAPH_STANDARDS.md binds the representation to one RDF graph in three layers joined by concept IRIs: a terminology backbone, a multi-modal instance layer, and a working property graph (what the explorer renders). The standard was written for medicine, the domain built first, so it names the medical vocabularies (MeSH canonical, with SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, UMLS and ICD cross-codes) and FHIR R4 for clinical records; the served graph already grounds other domains in their own vocabularies, such as FoodOn for foods and Wikipedia for general concepts. LAYERS.md separates the same system differently, into substrate (identity), connectivity (claims) and embeddings (one registered model per modality). Both are explained in Layers; the vocabulary is in RDF vocabulary and the code systems in Code systems.

A controller node The Cresco global controller for the region. External services The hosted LLM endpoint (Navigator, model lens), ORCID (sign-in), NCBI E-utilities (literature), upstream data hosts.

docs.title: Distributed by design
docs.text:
panAtlas is built as a distributed system on the Cresco agent mesh. Datasets join the atlas where they sit, each managed by its own cresco-panatlas plugin instance at the hosting site, and only structure crosses the mesh. The hub on the web host pulls every manager's report, shows them in the Mesh view, and folds permitted contributions into the graph. Remote panAtlas instances and computational resources are treated the same way, as peers on the mesh.

This documentation covers the mesh, federation contract, dataset managers, agents and operations in its own section, starting at Distributed.

docs.title: Knowledge layers
docs.text:
panAtlas separates what a thing is from what is claimed about it, and claims that panAtlas has verified from claims that were seeded from a source or derived by computation. The word "layer" is used for several of these separations in the repository. This page reconciles them with the code and states what lives in each layer today.

Sources: GRAPH_STANDARDS.md (decision record, adopted 2026-07-26, extended 2026-09-26), LAYERS.md, atlas/CLAUDE.md, and the build scripts and data at repo HEAD 57505c6. Counts were computed on 2026-11-10.

docs.title: Four uses of "layer"
docs.text:
Where Layers What it separates GRAPH_STANDARDS.md (1) terminology backbone, (2) clinical instance layer, (3) working property graph Kinds of content in the one RDF graph LAYERS.md substrate, connectivity, embeddings Identity, claims, and the models that produce claims The markdown atlas (atlas/CLAUDE.md) human-readable, machine-readable, evaluation, registry, governance pages Page types of the git-backed fact graph The layer attribute in graph.json foodatlas, concept, dataset, fndds, ontology, process, domain A display partition for the explorer (Graph schema)

These are not competing models. The first two describe the same graph from two angles (content type, and identity versus claim). The atlas is where curated, verifiable facts are written. The layer attribute is a user-interface grouping and carries no meaning beyond that.

      I["Layer 2: instance layer<br/>FHIR R4 for clinical records (designed)"]
    end
    subgraph CON["Connectivity (claims): edges with provenance"]
